sections.html:
Salem is a harbor city in Essex County on the North Shore, about 15 miles northeast of downtown Boston. The 2020 population was 44,480, spread over 18.3 square miles, and more than half of that area is water. Salem is mostly a residential and tourist city, and Salem State University, with more than 10,000 students, adds steady rental activity.

Salem Harbor, the North and South rivers and the Danvers River cut the city into small pieces. A house a few blocks away across a river can feel like a different neighborhood to a buyer, so say plainly which part of town yours is in.

  • Downtown: the historic core of the city.
  • Salem Neck and Winter Island: a peninsula northeast of downtown, home to the 30-acre Winter Island Park.
  • North Salem: west of the Neck, across the North River.
  • South Salem: south of the South River, mostly along Salem Harbor.

Beverly, Danvers, Peabody, Lynn, Swampscott and Marblehead all touch the city line. Public parks, harbor frontage and water leave limited land for new building, which keeps the supply of houses small.

Few Massachusetts cities carry as much preservation weight. Salem was a leading seaport in early American trade, and the 1692 witch trials still define its public image. Two residential areas, the Federal Street District and the Charter Street Historic District, are historic districts, and Chestnut Street is known for its Federal architecture.

The Great Salem Fire of 1914 destroyed more than 400 homes and left 3,500 families homeless, yet it spared the Chestnut Street block of Federal houses. Salem now has very old streets sitting beside blocks rebuilt in the early 1900s.

Owning inside one of those districts means exterior changes and teardowns may need city review, so the planning office is your first call. Pass what you learn to buyers. For any older house, a short list of when the roof, furnace and wiring were last done saves a round of questions.

sections.h2: Getting in and out of Salem
sections.html:
The MBTA Commuter Rail's Newburyport/Rockport Line stops in Salem. Routes 1A, 114 and 107 pass through the city, and Route 1A crosses the bridge to Beverly.

No highway runs inside the city. To reach Route 128, drivers take Route 114 into Peabody. Say so in the listing, because some buyers assume an exit is nearby.

A former rail line toward Marblehead is now a bike path, and the city has talked about a possible South Salem rail station on Ocean Avenue West. A house within walking distance of the train should lead with that.

sections.h2: What are Salem's short-term rental rules?
sections.html:
Salem regulates short-term rentals more tightly than most Massachusetts cities, a point worth checking if the house was ever listed on Airbnb or a similar site. The City of Salem short-term rental page explains the ordinances the City Council adopted in 2018. They require:

  • Annual registration of the rental with the city.
  • A Certificate of Fitness.
  • For a property that is not the owner's primary residence, a special permit from the Zoning Board of Appeals and registration for the non-owner-occupied trash fee.
  • Collection of the state and local room occupancy excise tax.

New non-owner-occupied short-term rentals are not permitted. The special permit path covers only properties that were already operating as short-term rentals before July 16, 2018, and zoning limits the use to certain neighborhoods.

That rule can decide what a buyer is allowed to do with the house. If you bought it as a short-term rental, confirm its registration and permit status with the city before you list, and have the paperwork ready for the buyer's attorney.

sections.h2: Before closing: alarm certificate and deed tax
sections.html:
Before a Salem house changes hands, the fire department has to sign off that its smoke and carbon monoxide alarms satisfy state rules. Book that visit the day your closing date is set. An alarm without a date stamp is treated as expired, and the department bills a fee for the inspection. The steps are laid out on the Mass.gov alarm page.

The deed excise tax comes from G.L. c. 64D, section 1, which names a base rate of $2 for each $500 of consideration. Let your closing attorney work out the figure and tell you who pays it at the table.

Tax due dates are printed on your bill. If the dates are unclear, call the assessor's office.

sections.h2: How to contest your Salem assessment
sections.html:
If you think Salem values your house above what it would really sell for, you can ask for an abatement, which is a cut to the bill. The value used is the one on January 1 ahead of the fiscal year. The steps are short:

  1. Keep every tax installment current.
  2. Hand the state-approved abatement form to the assessors no later than the first installment date on the bill.
  3. The assessors get three months to respond. Say nothing, and the request is deemed denied.
  4. If you disagree, take the case to the Appellate Tax Board inside three months.

The Appellate Tax Board publishes a guide that walks through each step. Bring sales of similar nearby houses to back up your number.

Smoke and CO certificateLocal fire departmentBook the visit when the closing date is set; a fee applies
Exterior work in a historic districtCity planning officeAsk before exterior changes or a teardown
Short-term rental statusCity of SalemConfirm registration and permit before listing

Abatement appealAppellate Tax BoardFile within three months of the assessors' decision

Gather these before you talk to any buyer: your latest tax bill, the date stamps on your alarms, any city permits for past work, and the short-term rental registration if one exists. Having them in a folder shortens every conversation and keeps small questions from turning into delays near the closing date.

sections.h2: What are your choices if you want to sell quickly?
sections.html:
Three routes exist: put the house on the market, sell without an agent, or take a cash offer. Listing works best for a house in good condition on a sought-after street. Cash tends to fit a home that needs work, an inherited property, or a landlord ready to exit.

Salem has its own sources of delay: a historic district review before exterior work, a question about transferring short-term rental status, or a wait for the fire department's alarm sign-off. Find out early which of these touch your house, then choose the route that dodges the slowest ones.

In a cash sale the buyer reviews the address, the condition and any liens or unpaid taxes, then makes an offer. Say yes, and a title company or attorney prepares the paperwork while the closing date follows your calendar. You skip showings, repair lists and the wait on a lender. Whatever offer you receive, work out what you would actually keep after commissions, repairs and the months of holding costs, and read the contract through before signing.

faqs.q: What county is Salem, MA in?
faqs.a: Salem sits in Essex County, north of Boston.

faqs.q: Is there a highway in Salem?
faqs.a: No. The nearest Route 128 access is along Route 114 in neighboring Peabody.

faqs.q: Can I run a short-term rental in Salem?
faqs.a: Only with city registration, a Certificate of Fitness and, for a non-owner-occupied unit, a special permit. New non-owner-occupied short-term rentals are not permitted.

faqs.q: Do I need a smoke and CO certificate to sell in Salem?
faqs.a: Yes. The local fire department must certify the alarms before a Salem house is sold or transferred.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Salem house in an historic district?
faqs.a: Yes. Check with the planning office before any exterior work, and tell buyers about any review that applies.
